narrative:
The model predicted a 64% chance that you would fail the bar exam on your first attempt. Because this probability is well above the acceptance threshold, your law school application was denied.

The decision was driven primarily by three factors, ranked by importance. Your third-year class ranking had the strongest influence, pushing the prediction strongly toward failure. Placing in the second decile is far below the average of roughly sixth-decile performance among students who were admitted, signaling consistent academic struggle in law school. Your LSAT score was the second most important factor and also pulled the outcome toward failure. A score of 25 sits well under the average of 37 seen in accepted applicants, indicating the exam measured gaps in the analytical skills the bar exam later tests.

Family income worked in the opposite direction. Coming from an upper-middle-income background slightly favored success, which aligns with the fact that most admitted students also come from similar or higher brackets. However, this positive effect was not large enough to overcome the academic signals.

Taken together, the model concluded that the combination of lower class rank and LSAT performance created too high a risk of bar exam failure. To improve your chances, focus on raising your academic performance and retaking the LSAT to demonstrate stronger analytical readiness. Consider targeted test-prep courses or academic support programs before reapplying.
